Q: Error CS9293: Cannot use an extension parameter in this context A:

The error occurs because extension parameters can only be used inside non‑static methods of the extension block. Static methods don't capture the extension parameter, so the compiler reports CS9293.

To fix it, remove the static modifier:

// removed 'static'
public int Baz() => bar % 2;

Q: How can I join two Git histories together A:

First, import all the histories in the same repository. In the most recent repository, do for the other one:

git remote add c:/path/toward/other/repository  
git fetch

Then :

git replace --graft <commit> <parent>

See https://stackoverflow.com/a/47938676/717372 for more details from a similar answer

Q: How to implement iterative two-stage optimization in CPLEX OPL controlled from Python? A:

I'm not familiar with CPLEX OPL, but I can guess from context that it is a third party solver.

Idealy of course, you would not write anything to a file. There are plenty of numerical solvers available for python, which would make it possible to do everything from python. That is of course, not always possible.

If you need to write intermediary results to files, then I'm pretty sure the format of the file does not matter much. You could use simple binary files, raw text, csv or json... Excel is fine, it wouldn't be my pick but use what you are confortable with.

As to how you could do this, I'm sorry but that looks like a sizable project. You might want to look into it yourself and ask any question you may have when they arise, but it is unlikely that someone will do it for you.

Q: What are the main differences between the dtplyr and dbplyr packages in their usage? A:

Both are wrappers that let you use dplyr syntax while leveraging higher-performance packages.

dtplyr translates to data.table code, which works primarily with data.tables, a variation of data frames. data.table is much faster than dplyr in certain cases -- I use it most often when I want to calculate by group and I have more than around 10,000 groups.

dbplyr translates to SQL, so you can query databases to generate data frames. Sometimes data is in a database and it's necessary (or at least more efficient) to do some filtering or aggregation before you bring the data into R.

Both packages have limitations, in that they aren't made to translate all dplyr code or work with all dplyr features (e.g. I think nested columns have been be one obstacle I've encountered), but can be useful for translating some of the most common functions.

(In the same vein, there are other packages like duckplyr, collapse, and arrow that can also help with handling very large data and/or getting higher performance than dplyr, while using the same / similar syntax.)
